```{r setup}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
set.seed(258)

plot_cols <- list(
  main        = "#1f4e79",
  main_dark   = "#16324f",
  secondary   = "#2563eb",
  accent      = "#d97706",
  red         = "#b91c1c",
  green       = "#047857",
  purple      = "#6d28d9",
  slate       = "#475569",
  text        = "#111827",
  muted       = "#4b5563",
  grid        = "#e5e7eb",
  border      = "#cbd5e1",
  shade_blue  = "rgba(37, 99, 235, 0.16)",
  shade_orange = "rgba(217, 119, 6, 0.22)",
  shade_grey  = "rgba(100, 116, 139, 0.14)",
  shade_green = "rgba(4, 120, 87, 0.14)"
)

make_region_poly <- function(x, y, xmin, xmax) {
  idx <- x >= xmin & x <= xmax
  data.frame(
    x = c(xmin, x[idx], xmax),
    y = c(0, y[idx], 0)
  )
}

make_tail_poly_right <- function(x, y, cutoff) {
  idx <- x >= cutoff
  data.frame(
    x = c(cutoff, x[idx], max(x[idx])),
    y = c(0, y[idx], 0)
  )
}

make_tail_poly_left <- function(x, y, cutoff) {
  idx <- x <= cutoff
  data.frame(
    x = c(min(x[idx]), x[idx], cutoff),
    y = c(0, y[idx], 0)
  )
}

plotly_slide_layout <- function(
    p,
    title,
    x_title,
    y_title,
    height = 340,
    x_range = NULL,
    y_range = NULL,
    shapes = list(),
    annotations = list(),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    legend_y = -0.18,
    margin = list(l = 64, r = 22, t = 48, b = 50)
) {
  p |>
    layout(
      title = list(
        text = paste0("<b>", title, "</b>"),
        x = 0.015,
        xanchor = "left",
        font = list(
          size = 20,
          family = "Arial, sans-serif",
          color = plot_cols$text
        )
      ),
      font = list(
        family = "Arial, sans-serif",
        color = plot_cols$text
      ),
      xaxis = list(
        title = list(
          text = paste0("<b>", x_title, "</b>"),
          standoff = 16,
          font = list(size = 15, color = plot_cols$text)
        ),
        range = x_range,
        tickfont = list(size = 13, color = plot_cols$muted),
        showline = TRUE,
        linewidth = 1.2,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showgrid = FALSE,
        ticks = "outside",
        ticklen = 5,
        tickcolor = plot_cols$border,
        automargin = TRUE
      ),
      yaxis = list(
        title = list(
          text = paste0("<b>", y_title, "</b>"),
          standoff = 18,
          font = list(size = 15, color = plot_cols$text)
        ),
        range = y_range,
        tickfont = list(size = 13, color = plot_cols$muted),
        showline = TRUE,
        linewidth = 1.2,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        gridcolor = plot_cols$grid,
        gridwidth = 1,
        ticks = "outside",
        ticklen = 5,
        tickcolor = plot_cols$border,
        automargin = TRUE,
        rangemode = "tozero"
      ),
      showlegend = showlegend,
      legend = list(
        orientation = "h",
        x = 0,
        y = legend_y,
        bgcolor = "rgba(255,255,255,0)",
        font = list(size = 13, color = plot_cols$text)
      ),
      shapes = shapes,
      annotations = annotations,
      margin = margin,
      paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
      plot_bgcolor = "white",
      hovermode = "closest",
      hoverlabel = list(
        bgcolor = "white",
        bordercolor = plot_cols$main,
        font = list(
          size = 13,
          color = plot_cols$text,
          family = "Arial, sans-serif"
        )
      ),
      height = height
    ) |>
    config(
      displaylogo = FALSE,
      displayModeBar = FALSE,
      responsive = TRUE,
      scrollZoom = FALSE
    )
}
```

## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

:::::: three-col
::: {.card .fragment}
[1 - Key Distributions]{.label} Normal, Chi-square, Student's $t$, and
$F$. Shape, parameters, and when each appears.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[2 - Sampling Distributions]{.label} Statistics have distributions too.
The CLT explains why the sample mean is (approximately) normal for large
$n$.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[3 - Law of Large Numbers]{.label} Sample averages converge to the true
mean. The mathematical bridge from data to probability.
:::
::::::

<br>

:::::: three-col
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
[Core skill]{.label} Identify which distribution applies and read
probability from it.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
[Core tool]{.label} R functions `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, `pchisq()`,
`pt()`, `pf()`.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
[Core habit]{.label} Check the degrees of freedom before looking up any
critical value.
:::
::::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What is Statistical Inference?

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Statistical Inference**

The aim is to produce **estimators** of population parameters based on a
smaller sample, and to quantify the accuracy of those estimators via a
probability statement.

We collect data from a **sample** → compute **statistics** → make
statements about the **population**.
:::

::::: two-col
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Classic inferential question**

"How sure are we that the sample mean $\bar{x}$ is close to the true
population mean $\mu$?"
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Why not measure everyone?**

Populations are usually infinite, very large, or expensive to enumerate.
Sampling + inference is the practical solution.
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Parameter, Statistic, and Sampling Variability {.scrollable}

:::::: two-col-wide
:::: col
::: taskbox
[Example]{.label} Suppose the true average commute time for all
UTM students is unknown.

A researcher takes **five different samples**, each with $n=25$
students, and computes a sample mean commute time for each sample.

**(a)** What is the population parameter?

**(b)** What statistic is computed from each sample?

**(c)** Why are the five sample means not exactly the same?

**(d)** What would happen to the sample means if each sample used
$n=200$ students instead?
:::
::::

::: col
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

set.seed(258)

sample_id <- rep(paste("Sample", 1:5), each = 25)
commute <- unlist(replicate(5, rgamma(25, shape = 5, scale = 8), simplify = FALSE))

df_commute <- data.frame(
  sample_id = sample_id,
  commute = commute
)

df_commute$sample_id <- factor(df_commute$sample_id, levels = paste("Sample", 1:5))
df_commute$x_num <- as.numeric(df_commute$sample_id)
df_commute$x_jitter <- df_commute$x_num + runif(nrow(df_commute), -0.11, 0.11)

means_commute <- aggregate(commute ~ sample_id, data = df_commute, FUN = mean)
means_commute$x_num <- as.numeric(means_commute$sample_id)
means_commute$x_left <- means_commute$x_num - 0.30
means_commute$x_right <- means_commute$x_num + 0.30

df_commute$tooltip <- paste0(
  "<b>", df_commute$sample_id, "</b>",
  "<br>One student commute time: ", round(df_commute$commute, 1), " minutes"
)

means_commute$tooltip <- paste0(
  "<b>", means_commute$sample_id, "</b>",
  "<br><b>Statistic:</b> sample mean",
  "<br>Sample mean commute time: ", round(means_commute$commute, 1), " minutes"
)

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_markers(
    data = df_commute,
    x = ~x_jitter,
    y = ~commute,
    text = ~tooltip,
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    name = "students in sample",
    marker = list(
      color = "rgba(80, 95, 105, 0.38)",
      size = 6
    )
  ) |>
  add_segments(
    data = means_commute,
    x = ~x_left,
    xend = ~x_right,
    y = ~commute,
    yend = ~commute,
    text = ~tooltip,
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    name = "sample mean",
    line = list(
      color = plot_cols$accent,
      width = 6
    )
  )

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "",
  x_title = "",
  y_title = "Commute time (minutes)",
  height = 390,
  x_range = c(0.55, 5.45)
) |>
  layout(
    annotations = list(
      list(
        x = 0.5,
        y = 1.08,
        xref = "paper",
        yref = "paper",
        text = "Dots are students. Thick lines are the sample means.",
        showarrow = FALSE,
        xanchor = "center",
        font = list(size = 12, color = plot_cols$main_dark)
      ),
      list(
        x = 0.5,
        y = -0.18,
        xref = "paper",
        yref = "paper",
        text = "",
        showarrow = FALSE,
        xanchor = "center",
        font = list(size = 12, color = plot_cols$main_dark)
      )
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      tickvals = 1:5,
      ticktext = paste("Sample", 1:5),
      showgrid = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      tickfont = list(size = 12)
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)",
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      tickfont = list(size = 12)
    ),
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0.5,
      xanchor = "center",
      y = 1.02,
      yanchor = "bottom",
      font = list(size = 11)
    ),
    margin = list(l = 60, r = 25, t = 75, b = 75)
  )|>
  layout(
    dragmode = FALSE,
    xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE)
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE
  )
```

## Sampling Variability - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

set.seed(258)

sample_means <- replicate(5, {
  commute <- rgamma(25, shape = 5, scale = 8)
  mean(commute)
})

sample_means
mean(sample_means)
sd(sample_means)

# Try changing 25 to 200 and compare the spread of the sample means.
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.1 The Normal Distribution

::::::: two-col-lean
::::: col
::: defbox
**Normal Distribution** — $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$$

for $-\infty < x < \infty$.

Parameters: mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2 > 0$.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
Also called the **Gaussian distribution**, after Carl Friedrich Gauss
(1809). It is symmetric and bell-shaped, completely characterized by
$\mu$ and $\sigma$.
:::
:::::

::: col
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

x_grid <- seq(-6, 10, length.out = 800)

df1 <- data.frame(x = x_grid, y = dnorm(x_grid, mean = -2, sd = 0.5))
df2 <- data.frame(x = x_grid, y = dnorm(x_grid, mean = 0, sd = 1))
df3 <- data.frame(x = x_grid, y = dnorm(x_grid, mean = 3, sd = 1.5))

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(
    data = df1,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "N(-2, 0.5²)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$green, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>N(-2, 0.5²)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df2,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "N(0, 1²)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$red, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>N(0, 1²)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df3,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "N(3, 1.5²)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$secondary, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>N(3, 1.5²)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  )

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "Normal distributions with different means and spreads",
  x_title = "x",
  y_title = "Density",
  height = 360,
  showlegend = TRUE
)|>
  layout(
    dragmode = FALSE,
    xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE)
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE
  )
```

## 4.1.1 The Standard Normal Distribution

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Standard Normal** — $Z \sim N(0, 1)$

$$f(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot e^{-z^2/2}$$

A special case with $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$. Denoted $Z$.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Standardising.** Any $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ can be converted:

$$Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0,1)$$

This lets us use a single table (or `pnorm()`) for any normal
distribution.
:::

```{=html}
<script>
window.empRuleUpdate = function () {
  var plot = document.getElementById("emp-rule-plot");
  var muSlider = document.getElementById("emp-mu-slider");
  var sdSlider = document.getElementById("emp-sd-slider");
  var muLabel = document.getElementById("emp-mu-label");
  var sdLabel = document.getElementById("emp-sd-label");

  if (!plot || !muSlider || !sdSlider || !muLabel || !sdLabel || !window.Plotly) {
    return;
  }

  var mu = Number(muSlider.value);
  var sd = Number(sdSlider.value);

  muLabel.innerHTML = mu;
  sdLabel.innerHTML = sd;

  function dnorm(x, mean, sigma) {
    return Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - mean) / sigma, 2)) / (sigma * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI));
  }

  var xmin = -15;
  var xmax = 15;
  var x = [];
  var y = [];

  for (var i = 0; i <= 900; i++) {
    var xVal = xmin + (xmax - xmin) * i / 900;
    x.push(xVal);
    y.push(dnorm(xVal, mu, sd));
  }

  function shadedTrace(a, b, color, name) {
    var start = Math.max(a, xmin);
    var end = Math.min(b, xmax);
    var sx = [];
    var sy = [];

    if (end <= xmin || start >= xmax) {
      return {
        x: [],
        y: [],
        type: "scatter",
        mode: "lines",
        fill: "tozeroy",
        fillcolor: color,
        line: { color: "rgba(0,0,0,0)" },
        hoverinfo: "skip",
        showlegend: false,
        name: name
      };
    }

    for (var j = 0; j <= 250; j++) {
      var sxVal = start + (end - start) * j / 250;
      sx.push(sxVal);
      sy.push(dnorm(sxVal, mu, sd));
    }

    return {
      x: sx,
      y: sy,
      type: "scatter",
      mode: "lines",
      fill: "tozeroy",
      fillcolor: color,
      line: { color: "rgba(0,0,0,0)" },
      hoverinfo: "skip",
      showlegend: false,
      name: name
    };
  }

  var data = [
    shadedTrace(mu - 3 * sd, mu + 3 * sd, "rgba(121,151,255,0.22)", "μ ± 3σ"),
    shadedTrace(mu - 2 * sd, mu + 2 * sd, "rgba(0,176,246,0.28)", "μ ± 2σ"),
    shadedTrace(mu - 1 * sd, mu + 1 * sd, "rgba(0,105,92,0.35)", "μ ± σ"),
    {
      x: x,
      y: y,
      type: "scatter",
      mode: "lines",
      line: { color: "#004d40", width: 3 },
      hovertemplate: "x=%{x:.2f}<br>density=%{y:.3f}<extra></extra>",
      name: "Normal curve",
      showlegend: false
    }
  ];

  var layout = {
    autosize: true,
    margin: { l: 42, r: 12, t: 8, b: 50 },
    xaxis: {
      range: [xmin, xmax],
      tickmode: "linear",
      tick0: -10,
      dtick: 2,
      zeroline: false,
      showgrid: false,
      title: ""
    },
    yaxis: {
      range: [0, 0.85],
      showticklabels: false,
      showgrid: true,
      gridcolor: "#e5e7eb",
      zeroline: false,
      title: ""
    },
    shapes: [
      {
        type: "line",
        x0: mu,
        x1: mu,
        y0: 0,
        y1: dnorm(mu, mu, sd),
        line: { color: "#f9a825", width: 2, dash: "dash" }
      }
    ],
    annotations: [],
    paper_bgcolor: "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor: "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    hovermode: "closest"
  };

  Plotly.react(plot, data, layout, { displayModeBar: false, responsive: true }).then(function () {
    Plotly.Plots.resize(plot);
  });
};

window.empRuleScheduleUpdate = function () {
  [60, 180, 420, 900].forEach(function (delay) {
    setTimeout(window.empRuleUpdate, delay);
  });

  requestAnimationFrame(function () {
    requestAnimationFrame(window.empRuleUpdate);
  });
};

window.empRuleScheduleUpdate();

window.addEventListener("load", window.empRuleScheduleUpdate);
window.addEventListener("resize", window.empRuleScheduleUpdate);
window.addEventListener("hashchange", window.empRuleScheduleUpdate);

if (window.Reveal) {
  Reveal.on("ready", window.empRuleScheduleUpdate);
  Reveal.on("slidechanged", function () {
    window.empRuleScheduleUpdate();
  });
}
</script>
```

## Normal Probabilities in R

::::::: two-col-lean
::: col
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# P(Z <= 1.96)
pnorm(1.96)

# P(Z > 1.96)   (right tail)
pnorm(1.96, lower.tail = FALSE)

# P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96)
pnorm(1.96) - pnorm(-1.96)

# Critical value: find z such that P(Z <= z) = 0.975
qnorm(0.975)
```
:::

::::: col
::: examplebox
**`pnorm(q, mean, sd)`** gives $P(X \le q)$.

**`qnorm(p, mean, sd)`** inverts: gives $q$ such that $P(X \le q) = p$.

Default: `mean = 0`, `sd = 1` (standard normal).
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Try it.** What is $P(X < 130)$ when $X \sim N(100, 15^2)$? Use
`pnorm(130, mean = 100, sd = 15)`.
:::
:::::
:::::::

## Example: Normal Probability with a Plot {.scrollable}

:::::: two-col-wide
:::: col
::: taskbox
[Example]{.label} Suppose final exam scores are approximately
normal with mean $\mu=72$ and standard deviation $\sigma=8$.

**(a)** Find the $z$-score for a score of $84$.

**(b)** Find $P(X \le 84)$.

**(c)** Find $P(X > 84)$.

**(d)** On the plot, identify the shaded right-tail region and explain
why it represents $P(X > 84)$.
:::
::::

::: col
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

mu <- 72
sigma <- 8
cutoff <- 84

x <- seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

df_norm  <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
df_left  <- subset(df_norm, x <= cutoff)
df_right <- subset(df_norm, x >= cutoff)

y_cut <- dnorm(cutoff, mu, sigma)
y_max <- max(y)

cut_col   <- "#4A5568"
left_col  <- "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.18)"
right_col <- "rgba(100, 116, 139, 0.20)"

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_norm,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    line = list(color = plot_cols$main, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0(
      "<b>Exam score:</b> ", round(x, 1),
      "<br><b>Density:</b> ", round(y, 4)
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_ribbons(
    data = df_left,
    x = ~x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = ~y,
    fillcolor = left_col,
    line = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Region:</b> P(X ≤ 84)",
      "<br><b>Meaning:</b> scores at or below 84",
      "<br><b>Area:</b> ", round(pnorm(cutoff, mu, sigma), 4),
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    visible = FALSE,
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_ribbons(
    data = df_right,
    x = ~x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = ~y,
    fillcolor = right_col,
    line = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Region:</b> P(X > 84)",
      "<br><b>Meaning:</b> scores above 84",
      "<br><b>Area:</b> ", round(1 - pnorm(cutoff, mu, sigma), 4),
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    visible = FALSE,
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_segments(
    x = cutoff,
    xend = cutoff,
    y = 0,
    yend = y_cut,
    line = list(color = cut_col, width = 2.5),
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Cutoff:</b> 84",
      "<br><b>z-score:</b> ", round((cutoff - mu) / sigma, 2),
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )

annotations <- list(
  list(
    x = cutoff + 1.8,
    y = y_cut * 1.22,
    text = "<b>x = 84</b>",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "bottom",
    font = list(size = 11, color = cut_col)
  )
)

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "Normal model for final exam scores",
  x_title = "Exam score",
  y_title = "Density",
  height = 360,
  x_range = c(min(x), max(x)),
  y_range = c(0, y_max * 1.15),
  annotations = annotations
) |>
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Normal model for final exam scores",
      x = 0.5,
      xanchor = "center",
      y = 0.96,
      yanchor = "top",
      font = list(size = 19)
    ),
    updatemenus = list(
      list(
        type = "dropdown",
        direction = "down",
        x = 0.03,
        y = 0.94,
        xanchor = "left",
        yanchor = "top",
        showactive = TRUE,
        bgcolor = "white",
        bordercolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.15)",
        borderwidth = 1,
        font = list(size = 11, color = "#2D3748"),
        buttons = list(
          list(
            label = "No shading",
            method = "update",
            args = list(
              list(visible = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)),
              list(title = list(
                text = "Normal model for final exam scores",
                x = 0.5,
                xanchor = "center",
                y = 0.96,
                yanchor = "top",
                font = list(size = 19)
              ))
            )
          ),
          list(
            label = "Show P(X ≤ 84)",
            method = "update",
            args = list(
              list(visible = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)),
              list(title = list(
                text = "Left-tail region: P(X ≤ 84)",
                x = 0.5,
                xanchor = "center",
                y = 0.96,
                yanchor = "top",
                font = list(size = 19)
              ))
            )
          ),
          list(
            label = "Show P(X > 84)",
            method = "update",
            args = list(
              list(visible = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)),
              list(title = list(
                text = "Right-tail region: P(X > 84)",
                x = 0.5,
                xanchor = "center",
                y = 0.96,
                yanchor = "top",
                font = list(size = 19)
              ))
            )
          )
        )
      )
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      showgrid = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      tickvals = c(40, 48, 56, 64, 72, 80, 88, 96, 104),
      tickfont = list(size = 11)
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)",
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      tickfont = list(size = 11)
    ),
    dragmode = FALSE,
    margin = list(l = 58, r = 20, t = 48, b = 52)
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE
  )
```

## Normal Probability - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

mu <- 72
sigma <- 8
x <- 84

z <- (x - mu) / sigma
z

pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)       # P(X <= 84)
1 - pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)   # P(X > 84)

pnorm(z)                              # same as P(X <= 84)
1 - pnorm(z)                          # same as P(X > 84)
```

## Example: Heights with Probability Plot {.scrollable}

:::::: two-col-wide
:::: col
::: taskbox
[Example]{.label} Adult heights in a population follow

$$
X \sim N(170, 8^2)
$$

where height is measured in centimetres.

**(a)** Find $P(X < 180)$.

**(b)** Find $P(X > 160)$.

**(c)** Find $P(162 < X < 178)$.

**(d)** Find the height $h$ such that only 5% of people are taller
than $h$.
:::
::::

::: col
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

mu <- 170
sigma <- 8

left_cut  <- 180
right_cut <- 160
mid_low   <- 162
mid_high  <- 178
h_cut     <- qnorm(0.95, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

x <- seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

df_height   <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
df_left     <- subset(df_height, x <= left_cut)
df_right    <- subset(df_height, x >= right_cut)
df_middle   <- subset(df_height, x >= mid_low & x <= mid_high)
df_top5     <- subset(df_height, x >= h_cut)

y_max     <- max(y)
y_left    <- dnorm(left_cut, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
y_right   <- dnorm(right_cut, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
y_mid_low <- dnorm(mid_low, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
y_mid_hi  <- dnorm(mid_high, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
y_h       <- dnorm(h_cut, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

mean_col  <- plot_cols$main_dark
curve_col <- plot_cols$main
cut_col   <- "#4A5568"

shade_col <- "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.18)"

left_col   <- shade_col
right_col  <- shade_col
middle_col <- shade_col
top_col    <- shade_col

ann_none <- list(
  list(
    x = mu,
    y = y_max * 1.08,
    text = "<b>Mean = 170 cm</b>",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    xanchor = "center",
    yanchor = "bottom",
    font = list(size = 12, color = mean_col)
  )
)

ann_left <- c(
  ann_none,
  list(
    list(
      x = left_cut + 1.2,
      y = y_left * 1.16,
      text = "<b>x = 180</b>",
      showarrow = FALSE,
      xanchor = "left",
      yanchor = "bottom",
      font = list(size = 11, color = cut_col)
    )
  )
)

ann_right <- c(
  ann_none,
  list(
    list(
      x = right_cut - 1.4,
      y = y_max * 0.62,
      text = "<b>x = 160</b>",
      showarrow = FALSE,
      xanchor = "right",
      yanchor = "middle",
      font = list(size = 11, color = cut_col)
    )
  )
)

ann_middle <- c(
  ann_none,
  list(
    list(
      x = mid_low - 0.8,
      y = y_mid_low * 1.14,
      text = "<b>x = 162</b>",
      showarrow = FALSE,
      xanchor = "right",
      yanchor = "bottom",
      font = list(size = 11, color = cut_col)
    ),
    list(
      x = mid_high + 0.8,
      y = y_mid_hi * 1.14,
      text = "<b>x = 178</b>",
      showarrow = FALSE,
      xanchor = "left",
      yanchor = "bottom",
      font = list(size = 11, color = cut_col)
    )
  )
)

ann_top5 <- c(
  ann_none,
  list(
    list(
      x = h_cut + 1.2,
      y = y_h * 1.16,
      text = paste0("<b>h ≈ ", round(h_cut, 1), " cm</b>"),
      showarrow = FALSE,
      xanchor = "left",
      yanchor = "bottom",
      font = list(size = 11, color = cut_col)
    )
  )
)

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_height,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    line = list(color = curve_col, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0(
      "<b>Height:</b> ", round(x, 1), " cm",
      "<br><b>Density:</b> ", round(y, 4)
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_ribbons(
    data = df_left,
    x = ~x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = ~y,
    fillcolor = left_col,
    line = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Region:</b> P(X < 180)",
      "<br><b>Meaning:</b> heights below 180 cm",
      "<br><b>Area:</b> ", round(pnorm(left_cut, mean = mu, sd = sigma), 4),
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    visible = FALSE,
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_ribbons(
    data = df_right,
    x = ~x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = ~y,
    fillcolor = right_col,
    line = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Region:</b> P(X > 160)",
      "<br><b>Meaning:</b> heights above 160 cm",
      "<br><b>Area:</b> ", round(pnorm(right_cut, mean = mu, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE), 4),
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    visible = FALSE,
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_ribbons(
    data = df_middle,
    x = ~x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = ~y,
    fillcolor = middle_col,
    line = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Region:</b> P(162 < X < 178)",
      "<br><b>Meaning:</b> heights between 162 cm and 178 cm",
      "<br><b>Area:</b> ", round(pnorm(mid_high, mean = mu, sd = sigma) - pnorm(mid_low, mean = mu, sd = sigma), 4),
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    visible = FALSE,
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_ribbons(
    data = df_top5,
    x = ~x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = ~y,
    fillcolor = top_col,
    line = list(color = "rgba(0,0,0,0)"),
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "<b>Region:</b> Top 5%",
      "<br><b>Meaning:</b> heights above h",
      "<br><b>Cutoff h:</b> ", round(h_cut, 2), " cm",
      "<br><b>Area:</b> 0.0500",
      "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    visible = FALSE,
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_segments(
    x = mu,
    xend = mu,
    y = 0,
    yend = y_max,
    line = list(color = mean_col, width = 2.2, dash = "dash"),
    hovertemplate = "<b>Mean:</b> 170 cm<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_segments(
    x = left_cut,
    xend = left_cut,
    y = 0,
    yend = y_left,
```

## Heights — Check in R with Plot

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

mu <- 170
sigma <- 8

# (a) P(X < 180)
pnorm(180, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# (b) P(X > 160)
pnorm(160, mean = mu, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)

# (c) P(162 < X < 178)
pnorm(178, mean = mu, sd = sigma) - pnorm(162, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# (d) 95th percentile because only 5% are above
qnorm(0.95, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# Plot the normal distribution and shade part (c)
x <- seq(mu - 4*sigma, mu + 4*sigma, length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

plot(x, y,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "#00695c",
     xlab = "Height in cm",
     ylab = "Density",
     ylim = c(0, max(y) * 1.08),
     yaxs = "i",
     main = "Normal model for adult heights")

shade_x <- x[x >= 162 & x <= 178]
shade_y <- dnorm(shade_x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

polygon(c(162, shade_x, 178),
        c(0, shade_y, 0),
        col = "#c8e6f3",
        border = NA)

lines(x, y, lwd = 2, col = "#00695c")
abline(v = mu, lty = 2, col = "#004d40", lwd = 2)
abline(v = c(160, 162, 178, 180), lty = 2, col = "#f9a825")
```

## 4.1.2 The Chi-Square Distribution

::: defbox
**Chi-Square Random Variable** — $X \sim \chi^2_k$

If $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_k \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)$, then

$$X = \sum_{i=1}^{k} Z_i^2 \sim \chi^2_k$$

The pdf for $x > 0$ is:

$$f(x; k) = \frac{1}{2^{k/2}\,\Gamma(k/2)}\, x^{k/2 - 1}\, e^{-x/2}$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
The distribution is **right-skewed** and supported on $(0, \infty)$. As
$k$ increases, it becomes more symmetric. $E[X] = k$,
$\text{Var}(X) = 2k$.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Chi-Square: Shape by Degrees of Freedom

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

x_vals <- seq(0.01, 15, length.out = 700)

df2 <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dchisq(x_vals, df = 2))
df5 <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dchisq(x_vals, df = 5))
df10 <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dchisq(x_vals, df = 10))

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(
    data = df2,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "χ²(2)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$green, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>χ²(2)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df5,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "χ²(5)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$red, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>χ²(5)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df10,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "χ²(10)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$secondary, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>χ²(10)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  )

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "Chi-square distributions by degrees of freedom",
  x_title = "x",
  y_title = "Density",
  height = 360,
  showlegend = TRUE
) |>
  layout(
    dragmode = FALSE,
    xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE)
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Key fact.** The chi-square distribution is always positive and
right-skewed. It plays a central role in tests for variance and for
categorical data (Chapter 7+).
:::

## Chi-Square in R

:::::: two-col-lean
::: col
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# P(X <= 10) where X ~ chi-sq(5)
pchisq(10, df = 5)

# Upper tail: P(X > 10)
pchisq(10, df = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Critical value: 95th percentile with df=10
qchisq(0.95, df = 10)

# Plot the distribution
ymax <- max(dchisq(seq(0, 20, length.out = 1000), df = 5))
curve(dchisq(x, df = 5), from = 0, to = 20,
      col = "#F8766D", lwd = 2,
      ylim = c(0, ymax * 1.08),
      yaxs = "i",
      main = "Chi-Square(5)", ylab = "Density")
```
:::

:::: col
::: defbox
**Mean & Variance**

For $X \sim \chi^2_k$:

$$E[X] = k, \qquad \text{Var}(X) = 2k$$

As $k \to \infty$, the chi-square distribution approaches a normal
distribution (by the CLT).
:::

## Example: Chi-Square Probability {.scrollable}

::: taskbox
[Example]{.label} Let $X \sim \chi^2_{8}$.

**(a)** Find $P(X \leq 15.507)$.

**(b)** Find the 95th percentile of $X$.

**(c)** If $Z_1, Z_2, Z_3 \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)$, what is
the distribution of $Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + Z_3^2$?

**(d)** What are $E[X]$ and $\text{Var}(X)$?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Chi-Square Example — Check in R with Plot

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Let X ~ chi-square with df = 8
df_value <- 8
cutoff <- 15.507

# (a) P(X <= 15.507)
pchisq(cutoff, df = df_value)

# (b) 95th percentile
qchisq(0.95, df = df_value)

# (c) sum of 3 squared standard normals is chi-square with 3 df

# (d) mean = k, variance = 2k
cat("Mean:", df_value, "  Variance:", 2 * df_value, "\n")

# Plot and shade P(X <= 15.507)
x <- seq(0, 30, length.out = 1000)
y <- dchisq(x, df = df_value)

plot(x, y,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "#00695c",
     xlab = "x",
     ylab = "Density",
     ylim = c(0, max(y) * 1.08),
     yaxs = "i",
     main = "Chi-square distribution with 8 df")

shade_x <- x[x <= cutoff]
shade_y <- dchisq(shade_x, df = df_value)

polygon(c(0, shade_x, cutoff),
        c(0, shade_y, 0),
        col = "#c8e6f3",
        border = NA)

lines(x, y, lwd = 2, col = "#00695c")
abline(v = cutoff, lty = 2, col = "#f9a825", lwd = 2)
```

##  {.quiz-question}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

$Z_1, Z_2, Z_3, Z_4 \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)$. What is the
distribution of

$$W = Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + Z_3^2 + Z_4^2 \; ?$$
:::

-   $W \sim N(0,4)$
-   $W \sim \chi^2_2$
-   [$W \sim \chi^2_4$]{.correct
    data-explanation="The sum of squares of k independent standard normal variables has a chi-square distribution with k degrees of freedom. Here k = 4."}
-   $W \sim t_4$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.1.3 The Student's $t$-Distribution

::: defbox
**Student's** $t$ Distribution — $T \sim t_\nu$

If $Z \sim N(0,1)$ and $U \sim \chi^2_\nu$ are **independent**, then

$$T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/\nu}} \sim t_\nu$$

The pdf is:

$$f_T(t;\nu) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\pi\nu}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} \left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}}, \quad -\infty < t < \infty$$
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
The $t$-distribution has **heavier tails** than the normal. As
$\nu \to \infty$, $t_\nu \to N(0,1)$.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## $t$ vs Normal: Heavier Tails

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

x_vals <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 700)

df_n  <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dnorm(x_vals))
df_t2 <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dt(x_vals, df = 2))
df_t9 <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dt(x_vals, df = 9))

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_n,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "Standard Normal",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$red, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>Standard Normal</b><br>Value: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_t2,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "t(2)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$green, width = 3.4, dash = "dash"),
    text = ~paste0("<b>t(2)</b><br>Value: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_t9,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "t(9)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$secondary, width = 3.4, dash = "dash"),
    text = ~paste0("<b>t(9)</b><br>Value: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  )

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "Student's t distribution has heavier tails than the normal",
  x_title = "Value",
  y_title = "Density",
  height = 360,
  showlegend = TRUE
) |>
  layout(
    dragmode = FALSE,
    xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE)
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Why does this matter?** When estimating a mean from a small sample
with unknown $\sigma$, we use $t$ critical values — they are larger than
$z$ values, reflecting extra uncertainty.
:::

::: {#t-tail-readout style="background:rgba(97,156,255,0.13); border-radius:7px; padding:8px 0; font-weight:800; font-size:1.25em;"}
P(\|T\| \> 2) = —
:::

::: {#z-tail-readout style="background:rgba(248,118,109,0.13); border-radius:7px; padding:8px 0; font-weight:800; font-size:1.25em;"}
P(\|Z\| \> 2) = —
:::
:::::
:::::::::

```{=html}
<script>
window.tTailUpdate = function () {
  var plot = document.getElementById("t-tail-plot");
  var dfSlider = document.getElementById("t-df-slider");
  var cutoffSlider = document.getElementById("t-cutoff-slider");
  var dfLabel = document.getElementById("t-df-label");
  var cutoffLabel = document.getElementById("t-cutoff-label");
  var tReadout = document.getElementById("t-tail-readout");
  var zReadout = document.getElementById("z-tail-readout");

  if (!plot || !dfSlider || !cutoffSlider || !dfLabel || !cutoffLabel || !tReadout || !zReadout || !window.Plotly) {
    return;
  }

  var nu = Number(dfSlider.value);
  var cutoff = Number(cutoffSlider.value);

  dfLabel.innerHTML = nu;
  cutoffLabel.innerHTML = cutoff.toFixed(1);

  function logGamma(z) {
    var x = [
      57.1562356658629235,
      -59.5979603554754912,
      14.1360979747417471,
      -0.491913816097620199,
      0.339946499848118887e-4,
      0.465236289270485756e-4,
      -0.983744753048795646e-4,
      0.158088703224912494e-3,
      -0.210264441724104883e-3,
      0.217439618115212643e-3,
      -0.164318106536763890e-3,
      0.844182239838527433e-4,
      -0.261908384015814087e-4,
      0.368991826595316234e-5
    ];

    var y = z;
    var tmp = z + 5.2421875;
    tmp = (z + 0.5) * Math.log(tmp) - tmp;

    var ser = 0.999999999999997092;

    for (var j = 0; j < x.length; j++) {
      ser += x[j] / ++y;
    }

    return tmp + Math.log(2.5066282746310005 * ser / z);
  }

  function tDensity(x, df) {
    var a = logGamma((df + 1) / 2);
    var b = logGamma(df / 2);
    var c = Math.sqrt(df * Math.PI);
    var d = Math.pow(1 + (x * x) / df, -(df + 1) / 2);

    return Math.exp(a - b) * d / c;
  }

  function normalDensity(x) {
    return Math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI);
  }

  function approxTwoTailT(df, c) {
    var step = 0.002;
    var area = 0;

    for (var x = c; x <= 20; x += step) {
      area += tDensity(x, df) * step;
    }

    return 2 * area;
  }

  function erf(x) {
    var sign = x >= 0 ? 1 : -1;
    x = Math.abs(x);

    var a1 = 0.254829592;
    var a2 = -0.284496736;
    var a3 = 1.421413741;
    var a4 = -1.453152027;
    var a5 = 1.061405429;
    var p = 0.3275911;

    var t = 1 / (1 + p * x);
    var y = 1 - (((((a5 * t + a4) * t) + a3) * t + a2) * t + a1) * t * Math.exp(-x * x);

    return sign * y;
  }

  function normalCdf(x) {
    return 0.5 * (1 + erf(x / Math.sqrt(2)));
  }

  function approxTwoTailZ(c) {
    return 2 * (1 - normalCdf(c));
  }

  var xmin = -6;
  var xmax = 6;
  var x = [];
  var yT = [];
  var yZ = [];

  for (var i = 0; i <= 900; i++) {
    var xVal = xmin + (xmax - xmin) * i / 900;
    x.push(xVal);
    yT.push(tDensity(xVal, nu));
    yZ.push(normalDensity(xVal));
  }

  function tailTrace(left, right) {
    var sx = [];
    var sy = [];

    for (var j = 0; j <= 250; j++) {
      var sxVal = left + (right - left) * j / 250;
      sx.push(sxVal);
      sy.push(tDensity(sxVal, nu));
    }

    return {
      x: sx,
      y: sy,
      type: "scatter",
      mode: "lines",
      fill: "tozeroy",
      fillcolor: "rgba(97,156,255,0.22)",
      line: { color: "rgba(0,0,0,0)" },
      hoverinfo: "skip",
      showlegend: false,
      name: "t tails"
    };
  }

  var data = [
    tailTrace(xmin, -cutoff),
    tailTrace(cutoff, xmax),
    {
      x: x,
      y: yZ,
      type: "scatter",
      mode: "lines",
      line: { color: "#f8766d", width: 2.4 },
      hovertemplate: "z=%{x:.2f}<br>density=%{y:.3f}<extra>N(0,1)</extra>",
      name: "N(0,1)"
    },
    {
      x: x,
      y: yT,
      type: "scatter",
      mode: "lines",
      line: { color: "#619cff", width: 2.8 },
      hovertemplate: "t=%{x:.2f}<br>density=%{y:.3f}<extra>t(" + nu + ")</extra>",
      name: "t(" + nu + ")"
    }
  ];

  var layout = {
    autosize: true,
    margin: { l: 42, r: 12, t: 8, b: 42 },
    xaxis: {
      range: [xmin, xmax],
      tickmode: "linear",
      tick0: -6,
      dtick: 1,
      zeroline: false,
      showline: true,
      linecolor: "#111111",
      linewidth: 2,
      showgrid: false,
      title: ""
    },
    yaxis: {
      range: [0, 0.45],
      showticklabels: false,
      showgrid: true,
      gridcolor: "#e5e7eb",
      zeroline: false,
      title: ""
    },
    shapes: [
      {
        type: "line",
        x0: -cutoff,
        x1: -cutoff,
        y0: 0,
        y1: tDensity(-cutoff, nu),
        line: { color: "#f9a825", width: 2, dash: "dash" }
      },
      {
        type: "line",
        x0: cutoff,
        x1: cutoff,
        y0: 0,
        y1: tDensity(cutoff, nu),
        line: { color: "#f9a825", width: 2, dash: "dash" }
      }
    ],
    legend: {
      orientation: "h",
      x: 0.02,
      y: 0.98,
      bgcolor: "rgba(255,255,255,0.7)"
    },
    paper_bgcolor: "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor: "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    hovermode: "closest"
  };

  var tTail = approxTwoTailT(nu, cutoff);
  var zTail = approxTwoTailZ(cutoff);

  tReadout.innerHTML = "P(|T| &gt; " + cutoff.toFixed(1) + ") = " + tTail.toFixed(4);
  zReadout.innerHTML = "P(|Z| &gt; " + cutoff.toFixed(1) + ") = " + zTail.toFixed(4);

  Plotly.react(plot, data, layout, { displayModeBar: false, responsive: true }).then(function () {
    Plotly.Plots.resize(plot);
  });
};

window.tTailScheduleUpdate = function () {
  [60, 180, 420, 900].forEach(function (delay) {
    setTimeout(window.tTailUpdate, delay);
  });

  requestAnimationFrame(function () {
    requestAnimationFrame(window.tTailUpdate);
  });
};

window.tTailScheduleUpdate();

window.addEventListener("load", window.tTailScheduleUpdate);
window.addEventListener("resize", window.tTailScheduleUpdate);
window.addEventListener("hashchange", window.tTailScheduleUpdate);

if (window.Reveal) {
  Reveal.on("ready", window.tTailScheduleUpdate);
  Reveal.on("slidechanged", function () {
    window.tTailScheduleUpdate();
  });
}
</script>
```

## $t$-Distribution in R

:::::: two-col-lean
::: col
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# P(T <= 2.0) with df = 10
pt(2.0, df = 10)

# Critical value: t such that P(T <= t) = 0.975, df=10
qt(0.975, df = 10)

# Compare to z critical value
qnorm(0.975)

# How many df until t ≈ z?
qt(0.975, df = c(5, 10, 30, 100, 1000))
```
:::

:::: col
::: examplebox
**`pt(q, df)`** → $P(T \le q)$

**`qt(p, df)`** → inverse CDF

Notice `qt(0.975, df=10) = 2.228` vs `qnorm(0.975) = 1.960`. The $t$
critical value is larger — reflecting extra uncertainty in small
samples.
:::
::::
::::::

## $t$ Example — Check in R with Plot

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# (a) P(T <= 2.131), df=15
pt(2.131, df = 15)

# (b) c such that P(-c <= T <= c) = 0.95, df=20
qt(0.975, df = 20)

# (c) P(|T| > 2.571), df=5
2 * pt(2.571, df = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)

# (d) 97.5th percentile comparison
qt(0.975, df = c(5, 30))
qnorm(0.975)

# Plot part (c): two tails for t with df = 5
df_value <- 5
cutoff <- 2.571

x <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 1000)
y <- dt(x, df = df_value)

plot(x, y,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "#00695c",
     xlab = "t",
     ylab = "Density",
     ylim = c(0, max(y) * 1.08),
     yaxs = "i",
     main = "Two-tail probability for t distribution")

left_x <- x[x <= -cutoff]
left_y <- dt(left_x, df = df_value)

right_x <- x[x >= cutoff]
right_y <- dt(right_x, df = df_value)

polygon(c(min(left_x), left_x, -cutoff),
        c(0, left_y, 0),
        col = "#c8e6f3",
        border = NA)

polygon(c(cutoff, right_x, max(right_x)),
        c(0, right_y, 0),
        col = "#c8e6f3",
        border = NA)

lines(x, y, lwd = 2, col = "#00695c")
abline(v = c(-cutoff, cutoff), lty = 2, col = "#f9a825", lwd = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Visual Question

The blue curve has heavier tails than the red normal curve. Why do we use
the $t$-distribution instead of the normal for small-sample inference about
a mean?
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
df_t <- 3

df_dist <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  normal = dnorm(x),
  t_dist = dt(x, df = df_t)
)

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_dist,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~normal,

  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_dist,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~t_dist,
    name = paste0("t distribution (df = ", df_t, ")"),
    line = list(
      color = plot_cols$main,
      width = 4.0
    ),
    text = ~paste0(
      "<b>Distribution:</b> t (df = ", df_t, ")",
      "<br><b>Value:</b> ", round(x, 2),
      "<br><b>Density:</b> ", round(t_dist, 4)
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  )

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "Normal curve compared with a t curve",
  x_title = "Standardized value",
  y_title = "Density",
  height = 300,
  x_range = c(-4, 4),
  y_range = c(0, 0.43)
) |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(
      showgrid = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      tickvals = seq(-4, 4, by = 1),
      tickfont = list(size = 12)
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)",
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      tickfont = list(size = 12)
    ),
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0.5,
      xanchor = "center",
      y = 1.12,
      yanchor = "bottom",
      font = list(size = 12)
    ),
    margin = list(l = 62, r = 25, t = 72, b = 55)
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = TRUE,
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = "reset",
    modeBarButtonsToRemove = c(
      "lasso2d",
      "select2d"
    )
  ) |>
  layout(
    dragmode = FALSE,
    xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE)
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE
  )

```

-   The normal distribution is only valid for large populations
-   [We must estimate $\sigma$ from the data, adding uncertainty — $t$ has heavier tails to account for this]{.correct
    data-explanation="For small-sample inference about a mean, the population standard deviation is usually unknown. Estimating it from the sample adds extra uncertainty, so the t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution."}
-   The $t$ is easier to compute
-   Small-sample data are always non-normal

## 4.1.4 The $F$-Distribution

::: defbox
$F$ Random Variable — $F \sim F_{\nu_1, \nu_2}$

If $U \sim \chi^2_{\nu_1}$ and $V \sim \chi^2_{\nu_2}$ are
**independent**, then

$$F = \frac{U/\nu_1}{V/\nu_2} \sim F_{\nu_1, \nu_2}$$

The $F$ distribution is supported on $(0, \infty)$ and characterised by
two degrees of freedom: **numerator** $\nu_1$ and **denominator**
$\nu_2$.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
The $F$ distribution is used to **compare two variances** and is the
backbone of **ANOVA** (Analysis of Variance). You will see it a lot in
later chapters.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## $F$-Distribution: Shape

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

x_f <- seq(0.01, 3, length.out = 700)

df_25   <- data.frame(x = x_f, y = df(x_f, 2, 5))
df_510  <- data.frame(x = x_f, y = df(x_f, 5, 10))
df_1030 <- data.frame(x = x_f, y = df(x_f, 10, 30))

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_25,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "F(2,5)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$green, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>F(2,5)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_510,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "F(5,10)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$red, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>F(5,10)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_1030,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~y,
    name = "F(10,30)",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$secondary, width = 3.4),
    text = ~paste0("<b>F(10,30)</b><br>x: ", round(x, 2), "<br>Density: ", round(y, 4)),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  )

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "F distributions with different degrees of freedom",
  x_title = "x",
  y_title = "Density",
  height = 345,
  y_range = c(0, 1.2),
  showlegend = TRUE
)|>

    dragmode = FALSE,
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# P(F <= 3) with df1=5, df2=10
```

##  {.quiz-question}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the
$\chi^2$ and $F$ distributions?
:::

-   $F$ is the square of a $\chi^2$ random variable
-   [$F$ is the ratio of two independent $\chi^2$ variables, each
    divided by its degrees of freedom]{.correct
    data-explanation="An F random variable is formed by dividing one chi-square variable by its degrees of freedom, then dividing by another independent chi-square variable divided by its degrees of freedom."}
-   $F$ is the sum of two $\chi^2$ random variables
-   $F$ is always symmetric like the normal

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary Table for Distributions

::: {.summary-table-slide}
| Distribution | Parameters | Support | $E[X]$ | Key use |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | $\mu, \sigma^2$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | $\mu$ | General continuous |
| $\chi^2_k$ | $k$ (df) | $(0,\infty)$ | $k$ | Variance tests |
| $t_\nu$ | $\nu$ (df) | $\mathbb{R}$ | $0$ | Small-sample mean |
| $F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}$ | $\nu_1, \nu_2$ | $(0,\infty)$ | $\dfrac{\nu_2}{\nu_2-2}$ | Variance ratios |

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Connections.** $Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1$; $\;$ $t_\nu^2 \sim F_{1,\nu}$;
$\;$ $t_\nu \to N(0,1)$ and $\chi^2_k/k \to 1$ as degrees of freedom
grow.
:::
:::

```{webr}
# --- Normal ---

mu <- 0; sigma <- 1; q <- 1.96
pnorm(q, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# --- Chi-square ---

# --- F ---
```

::: defbox
**Quick reference**

| Dist     | CDF      | Quantile |
|----------|----------|----------|
| Normal   | `pnorm`  | `qnorm`  |
| $\chi^2$ | `pchisq` | `qchisq` |
| $t$      | `pt`     | `qt`     |
| $F$      | `pf`     | `qf`     |

All accept `lower.tail = FALSE` for upper-tail probabilities.

## 4.2 Sampling Distributions

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Sampling Distribution**

The **probability distribution** of a statistic (such as $\bar{X}$)
computed from all possible random samples of a given size $n$ drawn from
the same population.
:::

::::: two-col
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Key idea.** $\bar{X}$ is not a fixed number — it is a **random
variable**. Each new sample of size $n$ gives a different value of
$\bar{X}$. The sampling distribution describes how those values vary.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Why it matters.** Understanding the variability of $\bar{X}$ from
sample to sample is the foundation for confidence intervals and
hypothesis tests.
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sampling Distribution of $\bar{X}$

::: defbox
**Distribution of the sample mean**

If $X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}$ population with mean
$\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, then:

$$E[\bar{X}] = \mu \qquad \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}$$

The **standard error** of $\bar{X}$ is
$\text{SE}(\bar{X}) = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
**Larger** $n$ → smaller SE. Collecting more data shrinks the
variability of the sample mean. This is why bigger samples give more
precise estimates.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sampling Distribution — Simulation

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Simulate sampling distribution of X-bar
# Population: Exponential(rate=1), mu=1, sigma^2=1

n     <- 30      # sample size
reps  <- 5000    # number of samples

xbar_vals <- replicate(reps, mean(rexp(n, rate = 1)))

h <- hist(xbar_vals, breaks = 50, plot = FALSE)
x_curve <- seq(min(h$breaks), max(h$breaks), length.out = 500)
y_curve <- dnorm(x_curve, mean = 1, sd = 1/sqrt(n))

hist(xbar_vals, breaks = h$breaks,
     col = "#00695c", border = "white",
     main = paste("Sampling distribution: n =", n),
     xlab = "Sample mean", freq = FALSE,
     ylim = c(0, max(h$density, y_curve) * 1.08),
     yaxs = "i")

# Overlay theoretical normal
lines(x_curve, y_curve, col = "#F8766D", lwd = 2)
```

::: small-text
Change `n` to 5 or 2 and re-run. Watch the distribution become less
normal.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Question

A population has mean 40 and variance 100. A random sample of size 25 is
drawn. What is the standard error of $\bar{X}$?
:::

-   10
-   4
-   [2]{.correct
    data-explanation="The variance is 100, so the standard deviation is sqrt(100) = 10. The standard error is 10 / sqrt(25) = 2."}
-   0.4

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.3 The Central Limit Theorem

::: defbox
**Central Limit Theorem (CLT)**

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with $E[X_i] = \mu$ and
$\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty$. Then as $n \to \infty$:

$$\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \;\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\; N(0,1)$$

Equivalently, for large $n$:
$\quad \bar{X}_n \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Remarkable.** The CLT holds for **any** parent distribution with
finite variance — uniform, exponential, Poisson, or anything else. The
shape of $\bar{X}$ approaches normal as $n$ grows.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## CLT: What "Large $n$" Means in Practice

:::::: three-col
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
[Symmetric distributions]{.label} Even $n = 10$–$15$ is often enough.
The normal approximation kicks in quickly.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
[Moderately skewed]{.label} $n = 30$ is a common rule of thumb. Check
with a histogram.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
[Heavily skewed]{.label} May need $n = 50$–$100$ or more. The more
extreme the skew, the larger $n$ must be.
:::
::::::

<br>

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Practical consequence.** For large $n$, we can use $z$-based
confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for $\mu$ even when the parent
distribution is unknown or skewed.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## CLT — Simulation Lab in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# CLT Simulator: change dist and n
dist <- "exponential"   # try: "uniform", "poisson", "exponential"
n    <- 30
reps <- 4000

draw_sample <- function(n) {
  switch(dist,
    uniform     = runif(n, 0, 1),
    exponential = rexp(n, rate = 1),
    poisson     = rpois(n, lambda = 3),
    rnorm(n)
  )
}

xbars <- replicate(reps, mean(draw_sample(n)))

# Theoretical parameters
mu_map    <- c(uniform=0.5, exponential=1, poisson=3, normal=0)
var_map   <- c(uniform=1/12, exponential=1, poisson=3, normal=1)
mu_t  <- mu_map[dist]; se_t <- sqrt(var_map[dist]/n)

h <- hist(xbars, breaks=50, plot=FALSE)
x_curve <- seq(min(h$breaks), max(h$breaks), length.out=500)
y_curve <- dnorm(x_curve, mu_t, se_t)

hist(xbars, breaks=h$breaks, freq=FALSE, col="#00695c", border="white",
     main=paste("CLT:", dist, "| n =", n), xlab="Sample mean",
     ylim=c(0, max(h$density, y_curve) * 1.08),
     yaxs="i")
lines(x_curve, y_curve, col="#F8766D", lwd=2)
```

## CLT Example: Poisson Sums {.scrollable}

::: taskbox
[Example]{.label} Customers arrive at a bank at rate $\lambda = 4$ per
minute. $X_i \sim \text{Pois}(4)$.

**(a)** What are $E[X_i]$ and $\text{Var}(X_i)$?

**(b)** For a sample of $n = 36$ one-minute intervals, find
$P(\bar{X} \leq 4.5)$ approximately.

**(c)** Find $P(\bar{X} > 3.8)$ approximately.

**(d)** What sample size $n$ would make
$P(|\bar{X} - 4| < 0.25) \geq 0.95$?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Poisson CLT — Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

mu <- 4; sigma2 <- 4; n <- 36
se <- sqrt(sigma2 / n)

# (b) P(X-bar <= 4.5)
pnorm(4.5, mean = mu, sd = se)

# (c) P(X-bar > 3.8)
pnorm(3.8, mean = mu, sd = se, lower.tail = FALSE)

# (d) P(|X-bar - mu| < 0.25) >= 0.95
# Need 2*pnorm(0.25/se_n)-1 >= 0.95
# 0.25/se_n >= 1.96  =>  se_n <= 0.25/1.96
# sigma/sqrt(n) <= 0.25/1.96
n_needed <- ceiling((2 * 1.96 / 0.25)^2)
cat("Minimum n:", n_needed, "\n")
```

## 4.4 Convergence in Probability

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Convergence in Probability**

A sequence $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ converges in probability to constant $c$
if for every $\varepsilon > 0$:

$$\lim_{n\to\infty} P\!\left(|X_n - c| \leq \varepsilon\right) = 1$$

Written $X_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} c$.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Intuition.** As $n$ grows, the probability that $X_n$ is far from $c$
shrinks to zero. The sequence settles down near $c$.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Chebyshev's Inequality

::: defbox
**Chebyshev's Inequality**

For any random variable $X$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, and
any $k > 0$:

$$P(|X - \mu| \geq k) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{k^2}$$

Equivalently: $P(|X - \mu| < k) \geq 1 - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{k^2}$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**No distributional assumption.** Chebyshev's inequality holds for
**any** distribution with finite variance. It is the key tool in proving
the WLLN.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Chebyshev Example {.scrollable}

::: taskbox
[Example]{.label} $X$ has mean $\mu = 10$ and standard deviation
$\sigma = 3$.

**(a)** Use Chebyshev to bound $P(|X - 10| \geq 9)$.

**(b)** Use Chebyshev to bound $P(1 < X < 19)$ from below.

**(c)** Now suppose $X$ is actually $N(10, 9)$. Compute the exact
probability $P(1 < X < 19)$ and compare with the Chebyshev bound.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Chebyshev — Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

mu <- 10; sigma <- 3

# (a) Chebyshev upper bound on P(|X-10| >= 9)
# k = 9
k <- 9
cheb_upper <- sigma^2 / k^2
cat("Chebyshev upper bound:", cheb_upper, "\n")

# (b) Lower bound on P(1 < X < 19) = P(|X-10| < 9)
cat("Chebyshev lower bound:", 1 - cheb_upper, "\n")

# (c) Exact (assuming X ~ N(10, 9))
exact <- pnorm(19, mean=10, sd=3) - pnorm(1, mean=10, sd=3)
cat("Exact (normal):", exact, "\n")
cat("Chebyshev is conservative — exact probability is higher.\n")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.4.2 Weak Law of Large Numbers

::: defbox
**Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN)**

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d. with $E[X_i] = \mu$ and
$\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty$. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$:

$$P\!\left(\left|\bar{X}_n - \mu\right| \geq \varepsilon\right) \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty$$

Written $\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \mu$.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
This does **not** say $\bar{X}_n = \mu$ for large $n$. It says the
probability of being far from $\mu$ goes to zero. Individual
realisations can still deviate.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Proof Sketch: WLLN via Chebyshev

::::::: two-col-lean
:::: col
::: examplebox
**Key steps**

1.  $\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$

2.  Apply Chebyshev with $k = \varepsilon$:

$$P\!\left(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| \geq \varepsilon\right) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}$$

3.  As $n \to \infty$, right side $\to 0$.

4.  Since probability $\geq 0$, conclude the limit is $0$. $\square$
:::
::::

:::: col
::: thinkbox
**What does the proof need?**

-   Finite variance $\sigma^2$
-   Independence (for $\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \sigma^2/n$)
-   Identical distribution (for common $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$)

The CLT is not required — Chebyshev alone is enough.
:::
::::
:::::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## WLLN — Simulation

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Watch the running mean converge to the truth
set.seed(42)
n  <- 200
p  <- 0.5    # true mean of Bernoulli(0.5)

x     <- rbinom(n, 1, p)
trial <- 1:n
rmean <- cumsum(x) / trial

plot(trial, rmean, type = "l", col = "#619CFF", lwd = 1.5,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "n", ylab = "Running mean",
     main = "WLLN: Bernoulli(0.5) running mean")
abline(h = p, lty = 2, col = "black")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## WLLN — Multiple Paths

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

set.seed(258)
n  <- 200; p <- 0.5
cols <- rainbow(8)

# First path
x <- rbinom(n,1,p); trial <- 1:n
plot(trial, cumsum(x)/trial, type="l", col=cols[1],
     ylim=c(0,1), xlab="n", ylab="Running mean",
     main="WLLN: 8 independent paths")

# Remaining paths
for(i in 2:8){
  x <- rbinom(n,1,p)
  lines(trial, cumsum(x)/trial, col=cols[i])
}
abline(h=p, lty=2, lwd=2, col="black")
```

## Example: Poisson WLLN {.scrollable}

::: taskbox
[Example]{.label} Let
$X_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 3)$ for
$i = 1, 2, \ldots$

**(a)** State $E[X_i]$ and $\text{Var}(X_i)$.

**(b)** Apply Chebyshev's inequality to bound
$P(|\bar{X}_n - 3| \geq \varepsilon)$.

**(c)** Show that $\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} 3$.

**(d)** Simulate the convergence in R for $n = 500$ trials.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Poisson WLLN — Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# (b)-(c): Chebyshev bound as function of n
lambda <- 3; eps <- 0.25; n_vals <- seq(10, 500, by=10)
bounds <- lambda / (n_vals * eps^2)

plot(n_vals, bounds, type="l", col="#F8766D", lwd=2,
     xlab="n", ylab="Chebyshev bound on P(|X-bar - 3| >= 0.25)",
     main="Chebyshev bound → 0 as n → ∞")
abline(h=0, lty=2)

# (d) Simulate
set.seed(1); n <- 500
x <- rpois(n, lambda)
plot(1:n, cumsum(x)/(1:n), type="l", col="#00695c", lwd=1.5,
     ylim=c(1,5), xlab="n", ylab="Running mean")
abline(h=lambda, lty=2)
```

```{r}
    x0 = 1,
    x1 = 120,
    y0 = 3.5,
    y1 = 3.5,
    line = list(color = plot_cols$accent, width = 2.4, dash = "dash")
  )
)

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "Law of Large Numbers for a fair die",
  x_title = "Number of rolls",
  y_title = "Running average",
  height = 285,
  x_range = c(1, 120),
  y_range = c(1, 6),
  shapes = shapes,
  margin = list(l = 64, r = 22, t = 52, b = 50)
)|>
  layout(
    dragmode = FALSE,
    xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE),
    yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE)
  ) |>
  config(
    displayModeBar = FALSE,
    scrollZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClick = FALSE
  )
```

-   3
-   6
-   4
-   [3.5]{.correct
    data-explanation="For a fair die, the expected value is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) divided by 6, which is 3.5. The Weak Law says the running sample mean converges in probability to that value."}

## Example: Law of Large Numbers {.scrollable}

:::::: two-col-wide
:::: col
::: taskbox
[Example]{.label} A fair coin is flipped many times. Let $X_i=1$
if the flip is heads and $X_i=0$ if the flip is tails.

The true population mean is:

$$
\mu = P(\text{Heads}) = 0.5
$$

**(a)** What does the running sample mean represent?

**(b)** Why does it jump around a lot at the start?

**(c)** What happens as the number of flips increases?

**(d)** Which result explains this behaviour?
:::
::::

::: col
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: "100%"

set.seed(258)

n_flips <- 2000
flips <- rbinom(n_flips, size = 1, prob = 0.5)

df_lln <- data.frame(
  flip_number = 1:n_flips,
  running_mean = cumsum(flips) / (1:n_flips),
  true_mean = 0.5
)

p <- plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_lln,
    x = ~flip_number,
    y = ~running_mean,
    name = "Running proportion of heads",
    line = list(
      color = plot_cols$main,
      width = 3.2
    ),
    text = ~paste0(
      "<b>Flip number:</b> ", flip_number,
      "<br><b>Running proportion of heads:</b> ", round(running_mean, 3)
    ),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_lines(
    data = df_lln,
    x = ~flip_number,
    y = ~true_mean,
    name = "True mean = 0.5",
    line = list(
      color = plot_cols$accent,
      width = 2.6,
      dash = "dash"
    ),
    hoverinfo = "skip"
  )

plotly_slide_layout(
  p,
  title = "",
  x_title = "Number of coin flips",
  y_title = "Running proportion of heads",
  height = 430,
  x_range = c(1, n_flips),
  y_range = c(0, 1)
) |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(
      showgrid = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      tickvals = c(1, 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000),
      tickfont = list(size = 12)
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)",
      showline = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      zeroline = FALSE,

    ),
    legend = list(

    ),

  ) |>
```

## Law of Large Numbers - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

set.seed(258)

flips <- rbinom(300, size = 1, prob = 0.5)
running_mean <- cumsum(flips) / seq_along(flips)

plot(running_mean,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     col = "#00695c",
     xlab = "Number of coin flips",
     ylab = "Running proportion of heads",
     main = "Law of Large Numbers")

abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "#f9a825", lwd = 2)

tail(running_mean)
```

## Empirical Probability Connection

::: defbox
**Empirical Probability from the WLLN**

Define indicator
$X_i = \mathbf{1}[\text{event } A \text{ occurs on trial } i]$.

Then $E[X_i] = P(A)$, and by the WLLN:

$$\bar{X}_n = \frac{\text{number of times } A \text{ occurs}}{n} \;\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\; P(A)$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Coin flip.** Tossing a fair coin: $P(\text{heads}) = 0.5$. After many
flips, the proportion of heads converges to $0.5$. This is precisely the
WLLN at work.
:::

## Chapter Summary {.compact}

:::::: three-col
::: {.card .fragment}
[Key Distributions]{.label} $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ for continuous data;
$\chi^2_k$ for variance; $t_\nu$ for small-sample means;
$F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}$ for variance ratios.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[CLT]{.label} For i.i.d. data with finite variance, $\bar{X}_n$ is
approximately $N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$ for large $n$, regardless of the
parent distribution.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[LLN]{.label} $\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\to} \mu$. Sample averages settle
near the population mean. Proof uses Chebyshev's inequality.
:::
::::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** The CLT and LLN together justify why
normal-based inference (confidence intervals, $t$-tests) works in
practice. Learn the distributions now — everything in Chapters 5+ builds
on them.
:::

## Bonus Example: Applying the CLT {.scrollable}

::: taskbox
[Bonus Example]{.label} Let $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$, so
$E[X] = 0.5$ and $\text{Var}(X) = 1/12$.

**(a)** For $n = 48$ i.i.d. draws, find $P(\bar{X} \leq 0.52)$
approximately.

**(b)** Find $P(0.48 \leq \bar{X} \leq 0.52)$ approximately.

**(c)** Simulate the sampling distribution and overlay the CLT
approximation. Do they agree?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bonus Example — Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n <- 48; mu <- 0.5; sigma2 <- 1/12; se <- sqrt(sigma2/n)

# (a) P(X-bar <= 0.52)
pnorm(0.52, mean=mu, sd=se)

# (b) P(0.48 <= X-bar <= 0.52)
pnorm(0.52, mu, se) - pnorm(0.48, mu, se)

# (c) Simulation
set.seed(42)
xbars <- replicate(5000, mean(runif(n)))
h <- hist(xbars, breaks=50, plot=FALSE)
x_curve <- seq(min(h$breaks), max(h$breaks), length.out=500)
y_curve <- dnorm(x_curve, mu, se)

hist(xbars, breaks=h$breaks, freq=FALSE, col="#00695c", border="white",
     main=paste("CLT: Uniform(0,1), n=", n), xlab="Sample mean",
     ylim=c(0, max(h$density, y_curve) * 1.08),
     yaxs="i")
lines(x_curve, y_curve, col="#F8766D", lwd=2)
```
